draft.body:
# A timetable is a promise

## Introduction

On the first morning of the bus pilot, I got to the library early enough to watch the lights come on. That is a small thing, but it explains why I care about this policy. A timetable is also a promise about whose time matters. Our campus should keep the evening shuttle for one more term while collecting better evidence, rather than calling a short pilot either a miracle or a failure. My own easier commute gives me a reason to ask the question; it does not answer it for everyone.

## Evidence

The transport office counted 240 boardings in the pilot week, compared with 160 in the earlier observation week. The shuttle therefore caused a 50 percent increase in student attendance. This result sounds decisive when I write it that way. Still, boardings are trips, and one rider can appear in the count several times. The two observation weeks also landed on different points in the semester. I want the numbers to earn their place in this paragraph rather than act like a badge that makes the argument official. The rider survey helps describe who answered, but it cannot tell us what every student needed.

## Recommendation

I would keep the route running while checking who can actually use it. The driver I spoke with called the last stop 'the long way home,' and that phrase stayed with me. It catches something the total number of rides misses: access has a shape as well as a size. Next term, the campus could count unique consenting riders, record missed connections, and invite comments from students who never board. This is a modest recommendation. I prefer a modest claim I can explain to a big claim that disappears when someone asks how we counted.

# A timetable is a promise

## Introduction

On the first morning of the bus pilot, I got to the library early enough to watch the lights come on. That is a small thing, but it explains why I care about this policy. A timetable is also a promise about whose time matters. Our campus should keep the evening shuttle for one more term while collecting better evidence, rather than calling a short pilot either a miracle or a failure. My own easier commute gives me a reason to ask the question; it does not answer it for everyone.

## Evidence

The transport office reported 240 boardings in the later week and 160 in the earlier one [@lyra:1]. However, these figures do not demonstrate a 50 percent increase in student attendance because they measure trips rather than unique individuals. A single rider can appear multiple times in the data, so the raw counts cannot isolate causal effects on overall campus attendance. Furthermore, the earlier counts were withdrawn because the counter recorded maintenance trips, and the current revision does not contain the old boarding totals [@lyra:1]. Since the revised data lacks the original totals, it cannot support claims about attendance trends. The rider survey presents a separate limitation: non-riders were not surveyed [@lyra:2]. Consequently, the responses describe only those who already use the shuttle and cannot establish demand across all students [@lyra:2]. I want to keep these numbers because they show the pilot is being used, but I do not want them to act like a badge that makes the argument official. The evidence supports further inquiry into how the shuttle is used, not a conclusion about its effect on overall campus attendance.

## Recommendation

I would keep the route running while checking who can actually use it. The driver I spoke with called the last stop 'the long way home,' and that phrase stayed with me. It catches something the total number of rides misses: access has a shape as well as a size. Next term, the campus could count unique consenting riders, record missed connections, and invite comments from students who never board. This is a modest recommendation. I prefer a modest claim I can explain to a big claim that disappears when someone asks how we counted.
